Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive inference by having a cheap draft model propose token sequences that a target model then verifies in parallel — the latency win comes entirely from the draft's acceptance rate, so anything that degrades draft quality directly attacks the speedup without touching accuracy. The central question here is: when an adversary (or simply a distribution shift) systematically degrades draft quality, how do you reshape the rejection sampling procedure to preserve the latency-accuracy Pareto frontier rather than watching it collapse? The key concepts are the token-level acceptance probability α (which governs both latency and the statistical guarantee that the output distribution matches the target), the correction distribution applied on rejection, and the tradeoff surface between average accepted tokens per forward pass and KL divergence from the target. What a beginner misses is that the standard guarantee — that speculative decoding is distribution-exact with respect to the target — is load-bearing: naive modifications to boost acceptance under a bad draft can silently corrupt the output distribution in ways that don't show up in perplexity or BLEU but matter enormously in calibration-sensitive or safety-critical applications. Experts also worry about the feedback loop: adaptive rejection policies that respond to draft degradation can themselves become attack surfaces if the adversary can observe or influence the acceptance signal.

In standard speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023), the correction distribution on rejection is defined as the normalized positive part of (p_target − p_draft), which requires p_draft to be a valid probability estimate of what the draft would sample — when p_draft is systematically biased (e.g., consistently underestimates probability mass on rare tokens), this residual distribution is no longer the right complement, and the composed output distribution drifts away from p_target even though the math looks correct token by token. The failure mode is insidious: unlike noise, which washes out in expectation, bias introduces a consistent directional error into the correction term, meaning every rejected token pulls the output distribution in the same wrong direction — this is distribution corruption, not variance inflation. Concretely, if a degraded draft systematically suppresses low-frequency tokens (a known failure mode of quantized or pruned draft models, documented in the context of LLaMA-based speculative setups), the correction distribution over-concentrates on those tokens at rejection, producing output that is more peaked on rare tokens than p_target intends — the opposite of the safety margin practitioners assume they have. SpecTr (Sun et al., 2023) and related optimal-transport framings make this precise: the acceptance-correction mechanism is only distribution-exact when draft probabilities are drawn from a consistent estimator of the true draft distribution; a biased estimator breaks the coupling argument entirely. Practically, this means that in adversarial degradation scenarios, the system can silently pass distributional audits (the marginal token distribution looks close to target) while the conditional distribution — what comes after a rejection event — is systematically wrong, which is exactly what matters for coherence and factuality in multi-step generation.

The bound that prevents unbounded steering is the total variation distance between p_target and the correction distribution's support: the correction term is clipped to the positive part of (p_target − p_draft), so the adversary cannot inject probability mass into tokens where p_target is zero, and can only amplify tokens where p_target already has support — the target model's own distribution is a hard envelope. However, within that envelope the attack has real leverage: if p_target assigns even small but nonzero probability to a harmful or specific token t*, the adversary can engineer near-certain rejection on the preceding context and make the correction distribution's normalized mass concentrate heavily on t*, achieving effective steering toward low-probability-but-nonzero target outputs without ever exceeding the TV bound. This is closely related to the "speculative decoding as a sampler manipulation" framing explored informally in alignment contexts (e.g., discussions around Anthropic's internal red-teaming of inference-time interventions) and more formally connects to backdoor attacks on samplers studied in the adversarial ML literature, where small distributional shifts at inference time compound across tokens. The practical bound is therefore not TV distance alone but the minimum p_target assigns to the adversary's target tokens — models with sharper, more confident distributions (lower temperature, or naturally low entropy on the relevant context) are paradoxically more resistant because there's less residual mass in the correction term to exploit, while well-calibrated but uncertain models are the most vulnerable.

This is operationally similar to the anomaly detection approach used in SpecInfer (Miao et al., 2023) and related systems where draft quality is monitored to switch between speculation depths, except here the signal is not just mean acceptance rate but the distributional shape of α_t over a window — an adversarial sequence will show bimodal acceptance (very high and very low) rather than the unimodal degraded-but-uniform profile of a merely bad draft. The detection problem has a known fundamental limit from sequential hypothesis testing: the Wald SPRT gives the optimal sample complexity for distinguishing the two regimes, and for realistic adversarial miscalibration (say, draft bias of 0.15-0.3 in TV distance, which corresponds to aggressive but not implausible degradation), detection lags of 10-30 tokens are achievable at false positive rates below 1% — short enough to intervene before multi-sentence coherence is compromised. The residual blind spot is that a sophisticated adversary who knows the detector's window size and threshold can craft a slow drift attack that keeps the acceptance ratio sequence just below the detection boundary, spending their manipulation budget across more tokens to stay under the CUSUM threshold — this arms race between drift rate and detection sensitivity is the inference-time analog of the epsilon-ball evasion problem in adversarial examples.

Increasing window size is a losing strategy in the limit: a slow-drift adversary with knowledge of the window W can always spread manipulation across W+1 tokens to stay below threshold, so the defender's detection delay scales linearly with W while the adversary's cost scales only logarithmically (they need finer-grained control but not proportionally more budget) — this asymmetry means the arms race favors the adversary as W grows. A practical hybrid is to run two detectors in parallel: a short-window (W≈5) sensitive detector that triggers a lightweight intervention (temporarily dropping to target-only greedy decoding, no speculation) and a long-window (W≈50) high-specificity detector that triggers a harder response (flagging the session, rejecting the draft model entirely) — the short window catches fast attacks at the cost of false positives, while the long window provides high-confidence attribution for slow attacks, accepting that some semantic damage has occurred but limiting its extent. The irreducible vulnerability is that for sufficiently slow drift — manipulation spread across hundreds of tokens — no online detector with bounded memory can distinguish adversarial slow drift from genuine distribution shift in the input domain, and at that point the problem has left the inference-time security layer entirely and become a question of whether the deployment pipeline can detect draft model compromise offline before it accumulates.
